exercises.title: 📝 API Changelog Writing
exercises.subtitle: Master the Keep a Changelog standard: entry categories, breaking change language, active voice style, and reading version sequences. Intermediate

questions.q: Which changelog entry correctly follows the Keep a Changelog standard for a newly added endpoint?
options: "## [2.3.0] - 2025-03-15 ### Added - `POST /payments/refund`: Initiates a refund for a completed order. Required fields: `order_id`, `amount_cents`, `reason`. Returns a refund object with id, status, and estimated processing time."
"New feature: we added a refund endpoint so you can now initiate refunds! This was highly requested by the community."
"[ADDED] POST /payments/refund - initiates a refund for a completed order; added 2025-03-15"
"Added POST /payments/refund (2025-03-15)" - inline date, no section heading, no version block.
questions.explanation: Option A correctly follows the Keep a Changelog format. This standard is widely adopted for APIs because it creates machine-parseable, developer-friendly change history. Required element Format In Option A Version header ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD ## [2.3.0] - 2025-03-15 Category heading ### Added / Changed / Deprecated / Removed / Fixed / Security ### Added Bullet entry Active voice, specific, with context - `POST /payments/refund`: Initiates a refund… Technical specifics What fields, what it returns, what it does Required fields, return object described The six Keep a Changelog categories: Added - new features, new endpoints, new fields Changed - changes to existing functionality Deprecated - soon-to-be removed features (give timeline) Removed - removed features (previously deprecated) Fixed - bug fixes Security - fixes to security vulnerabilities

questions.q: A bug caused the total_amount response field in GET /orders/{id} to return values in cents (e.g. 1999 ) instead of dollars (e.g. 19.99 ) for the past three months. This has now been corrected. Under which Keep a Changelog category should this correction be documented?
options: Deprecated - the old cents-based return behaviour was a legacy format that is now being formally deprecated in favour of the correct dollar format.
Changed - the format of the total_amount field was altered, which is a change to the API response contract.

Fixed - this is a bug correction. The field was returning incorrect data due to a defect. "Fixed" is for corrections to unintended behaviour. "Changed" is for intentional modifications. Since the original design intent was dollars, restoring to that behaviour is a fix, not a change.
Removed - the cents-based return value should be documented as Removed; the dollar-based return should be documented as Added.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct. The key distinction is intent : was the previous behaviour the designed behaviour (then a "Changed" entry documents the intentional departure) or a defect (then "Fixed" is correct)? Category Use when Example Fixed The previous behaviour was a bug - not what was designed or documented total_amount returning cents instead of dollars (spec always said dollars) Changed The previous behaviour was intentional and is now intentionally different Changing total_amount to return cents as a deliberate design decision (breaking change - needs version bump) Important nuance: A "Fixed" entry that corrects existing behaviour can still be a breaking change in practice - consumers may have written code that worked around the bug. The example here (returning cents when dollars were documented) likely means some consumers are already dividing by 100 as a workaround. A well-written Fixed entry acknowledges this: "Fixed: total_amount now returns dollar values as documented. Note: if your integration divides this value by 100 as a workaround, that workaround should be removed."

questions.q: Which changelog entry most clearly communicates a breaking change to developers scanning the changelog?
options: "## [3.0.0] - 2025-06-01 ### Removed - **BREAKING**: `GET /v2/products` has been removed. Use `GET /v3/products` instead. The `category_ids` array field replaces the deprecated `category_id` string field. Update all integrations before 2025-06-01. Migration guide: [link]."
"v3.0 is now live! We've made several improvements to the products endpoint including better category support."
"### Changed - Updated the products endpoint to v3 with improved performance and category handling."
"The products API has been modernised. Please update your integration to use the new endpoint."
questions.explanation: Option A contains every element required for a breaking change entry that developers can act on. Entries B, C, and D fail in specific ways: Entry What's missing B - "v3.0 is now live!" No breaking change label; sounds like a minor enhancement; no action guidance C - "Updated to v3" Under "Changed" not "Removed"; no specifics; no migration path; no urgency D - "has been modernised" Vague marketing language; no technical specifics; no date; no action required What makes Option A work: ## [3.0.0] - major version increment signals breaking change in SemVer ### Removed - correct category; the endpoint is gone, not changed BREAKING - explicit keyword for engineers scanning changelogs Old endpoint named + new endpoint named - reduces ambiguity Field migration explained - category_ids replaces category_id Deadline - "before 2025-06-01" creates urgency for sprint planning Migration guide linked - detailed instructions one click away

questions.q: Which writing style is standard for individual Keep a Changelog bullet entries?
options: "The cache headers were updated by the engineering team to include ETag support for conditional GET requests."
"Updated cache headers to include ETag support for conditional GET requests."
"Cache headers: it was decided that ETag support should be added to improve conditional GET performance."
"We are happy to announce that cache headers have been improved with ETag support following community feedback."
questions.explanation: Option B is the standard style: active voice , imperative/past tense action verb at the start, specific change described, no filler words. Style issue Options A, C, D Option B Voice Passive ("were updated", "was decided") Active ("Updated") Agent mention "by the engineering team", "we are happy" - unnecessary No agent - the change is the subject Filler phrases "we are happy to announce", "it was decided" None - goes straight to the change Specificity A is specific; C and D are vague about what ETag support means Specific: what changed (cache headers + ETag) and why it matters (conditional GET) Changelog entry formula: [Action verb] [what changed] [why or what it enables] [if needed: affected versions/endpoints] Examples of well-formatted entries: ✓ "Added cursor field to all paginated list responses for cursor-based pagination." ✓ "Fixed race condition in POST /transactions that could cause duplicate charges on network timeout." ✓ "Deprecated GET /v2/customers . Use GET /v3/customers . Sunset date: 2026-01-01."

questions.q: A changelog shows these entries in reverse chronological order: v2.1.3 (today), v2.1.2, v2.1.1, v2.0.0 - with no v2.1.0 entry anywhere in the file. What does the absence of a v2.1.0 entry most likely signal?
options: v2.1.0 was intentionally skipped for superstitious or marketing reasons - some projects deliberately skip certain version numbers.

v2.1.0 was likely released but had a critical bug discovered immediately after and was yanked (pulled from public availability) before reaching wide deployment. v2.1.1 was the rapid hotfix. This is a normal pattern in fast-moving projects; some teams document yanked releases with a [YANKED] tag in the changelog.
v2.1.0 was tested internally and passed to staging but was never released to production; only even patch versions are released publicly.
The changelog has errors - every released version must appear in the changelog, and a missing v2.1.0 entry means the team is not following semantic versioning correctly.
questions.explanation: Option B describes the most common and technically accurate explanation for a missing version in an otherwise sequential changelog. The [YANKED] tag is the Keep a Changelog convention for this situation: Keep a Changelog convention Usage [YANKED] tag Added to a version entry to signal it was pulled from distribution. Example: ## [2.1.0] - 2025-03-01 [YANKED] Why document yanked versions? Preserves audit trail; explains the gap in the version sequence; helps users who managed to install the yanked version understand they need to upgrade Reading a changelog as a senior engineer: A jump from v2.0.0 directly to v2.1.1 is a yellow flag - worth noting when evaluating a dependency A major version jump (v1.x → v2.0.0) always means breaking changes and should prompt a review of the migration guide Many minor patch versions in rapid succession (v2.1.1, v2.1.2, v2.1.3 within a week) may indicate instability in a release area Long gaps between versions are common for stable, well-designed APIs - they indicate the API contract is settled

questions.q: Sarah from the backend team posted this message in Slack after reviewing a pull request that added a new user authentication endpoint: "Okay, I've reviewed the changes to /auth/register . The PR includes a new field, user_metadata , which allows users to store custom data. I'm happy with this addition. Just a note: we should definitely update the API documentation to reflect this change."
options: incorrect - the message is too vague and doesn't convey enough information about the change.
insufficient - the pull request doesn't specify the impact of the change.
incorrect - Sarah should have focused solely on testing the functionality, not documenting it.
correct - the message clearly states the new feature and indicates a need for documentation updates.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the importance of proactive communication in a code review. While documentation updates are often necessary after new features are added, Sarah's message effectively communicates that a change has been made (the addition of `user_metadata`) and suggests a relevant action - updating the API documentation. The other options misrepresent Sarah's role or fail to acknowledge the need for clear communication about API updates.

questions.q: PR Description During a code review for a new payment processing endpoint, David writes the following description for his pull request: "Added support for accepting payments via Stripe. This includes a new `stripe_secret_key` parameter in the `/payments` route and updates to the webhook handling logic. We've also added some logging around successful and failed transactions."
options: Clear and concise - it effectively summarizes the changes, including new parameters and webhook updates.
Acceptable - it provides a basic overview but could benefit from more technical specifics.
Poor - it doesn't mention any potential breaking changes or rate limits.
Insufficient - the description lacks detail about the API response format.
questions.explanation: The correct option highlights that the description is clear and concise. A good PR description should quickly convey the purpose of the change, including new parameters, logic updates, and any relevant considerations like rate limits or potential breaking changes. The other options present misconceptions: simply stating 'it's clear' doesn't assess the quality; lacking detail is insufficient; and failing to address breaking changes or rate limits would be poor practice. David's description strikes a good balance between brevity and essential information.

questions.q: Mark is working on updating the API changelog for a new feature: a real-time chat endpoint. He's noticed that several recent entries are too verbose and lack specific details about *why* the change was made. During a code review discussion, his teammate, Emily, suggests he should focus on clarity and impact. Which of the following statements best reflects Mark's responsibility when writing API changelog entries according to Keep a Changelog principles?
options: Insufficient - Mark's primary focus should be on adhering strictly to the format guidelines without considering context.
Sufficient - Mark needs to clearly articulate the *reason* behind each change, focusing on the problem being solved and the value delivered.
Sufficient - Mark should prioritize listing every change regardless of its impact or reason.
Insufficient - Mark should simply list all the technical details of the changes for completeness.
questions.explanation: Keep a Changelog emphasizes communicating the *why* behind changes. While listing technical details is important, the core principle is to explain the problem being addressed and the value provided by the change. Option D incorrectly suggests simply listing everything; option C ignores the core purpose of Keep a Changelog. Option A misinterprets the guidelines, prioritizing format over clarity. The correct answer focuses on articulating the reason for the change - this aligns with the principles of transparency and understanding.

questions.q: David is reviewing a pull request for a new payment processing endpoint. He's noticed the changelog entry for the addition of Stripe support is quite detailed, listing all the changes - the `stripe_secret_key` parameter, webhook updates, and logging. However, his teammate, Emily , points out that the changelog should focus on the *impact* of the change rather than simply describing what was added. Which of the following best reflects David's responsibility according to Keep a Changelog principles in this situation? Option D: The changelog entry is perfectly acceptable as it provides a comprehensive overview of all technical changes. Option B: David should remove the details about the webhook updates and logging, focusing solely on adding the `stripe_secret_key` parameter to keep the changelog concise. Option A: David should rewrite the changelog entry to clearly state how this change improves payment processing, highlighting the benefits for users and developers. Option C: David should add a separate section to the changelog detailing the technical implementation details of the Stripe integration, regardless of its relevance to consumers.
options: Option A: David should rewrite the changelog entry to clearly state how this change improves payment processing, highlighting the benefits for users and developers.
Option B: David should remove the details about the webhook updates and logging, focusing solely on adding the `stripe_secret_key` parameter to keep the changelog concise.
Option C: David should add a separate section to the changelog detailing the technical implementation details of the Stripe integration, regardless of its relevance to consumers.
Option D: The changelog entry is perfectly acceptable as it provides a comprehensive overview of all technical changes.
questions.explanation: The core principle of Keep a Changelog is to focus on the *impact* of changes rather than simply listing what was added or modified. Option A aligns with this by emphasizing communicating the benefits and how the change improves functionality. Options D and B incorrectly suggest detailed technical descriptions are always necessary, while option C deviates from the standard by creating an unstructured section. This demonstrates understanding that changelogs should be easily digestible for developers who need to quickly understand the implications of a new API version.

exercises.title: 📅 API Deprecation Communication
exercises.subtitle: Master vocabulary for API deprecation: lifecycle phases, HTTP deprecation headers, migration guides, consumer notification strategy, and breaking change announcements. Intermediate

questions.q: An API team is planning to retire the v1 /auth/token endpoint. Which sequence correctly describes the standard API deprecation lifecycle?
options: Announce deprecation → enter soft deprecation period (endpoint still works but returns deprecation warnings in headers and changelog) → publish a sunset date → hard removal on or after the sunset date. Consumers are given sufficient time to migrate between each phase.
Skip any notice period and immediately replace v1 with v2 - backward compatibility is the consumer's responsibility, not the provider's.
Deprecation only applies to major API versions - individual endpoints within a minor version can be removed at any time without a deprecation process.
Hard-code an end date into the API - automatically return 410 Gone on the sunset date without any prior warning to consumers.
questions.explanation: Option A describes the industry-standard deprecation lifecycle. Skipping phases creates consumer trust problems and potential business and contractual damage for external APIs: Phase What happens Consumer action 1. Announcement Deprecation notice published: changelog, email, dashboard banner, API docs updated Begin planning migration 2. Soft deprecation Endpoint still works; Deprecation header added to responses; warnings in developer console Monitoring tools alert engineering teams; migration begins 3. Sunset date published Sunset header added to responses; final notices sent Complete migration before the date 4. Hard removal Endpoint returns 410 Gone or is removed from routing Any remaining integrations break - migration window has closed Timeline guidance: For widely-used public APIs, 6-12 months between announcement and hard removal is standard. For internal APIs with known consumers, 90 days is often sufficient. For APIs with large enterprise customers or SLA obligations, longer timelines and direct migration support may be required.

questions.q: An API starts returning two response headers: Deprecation: Sat, 01 Jan 2026 00:00:00 GMT and Sunset: Sat, 01 Jul 2026 00:00:00 GMT . What information do these headers communicate to API clients and their tooling?
options: The Deprecation header shows the date the current API version was first released; Sunset shows the date the next version will be released.
Deprecation marks the endpoint as legacy but provides no action timeline; Sunset announces a new feature release date.
These are security headers - Deprecation indicates when the TLS certificate expires; Sunset indicates a scheduled maintenance window.

Deprecation signals that the endpoint was deprecated as of the given date - consumers should begin migrating. Sunset signals the date on or after which the endpoint may be removed, providing a hard migration deadline. Together, they enable monitoring tools and SDKs to alert engineering teams automatically about approaching deprecation deadlines.
questions.explanation: Option D correctly describes both headers. The Deprecation and Sunset headers are defined in IETF drafts (draft-dalal-deprecation-header and RFC 8594) and are specifically designed for machine-readable deprecation signalling: Header Value format Meaning Deprecation HTTP-date or true This endpoint is deprecated as of this date. Begin migration. Sunset HTTP-date This endpoint will be removed on or after this date. Hard deadline. Link (companion) rel="deprecation" or rel="successor-version" Link to documentation about the deprecation or the replacement endpoint Why headers beat documentation alone: Deprecation headers can be parsed programmatically - API observability tools (Datadog, New Relic, custom dashboards) can automatically detect when a service makes calls to a deprecated endpoint and alert the owning team. This is far more effective than expecting developers to read changelogs proactively.

questions.q: A deprecation notice for the v1/orders endpoint includes a link to a "migration guide." What must a migration guide contain to be genuinely useful to API consumers?
options: A migration guide is optional for small breaking changes - for minor field renames, a changelog entry is sufficient and no guide is necessary.
A one-paragraph announcement stating that v1 is deprecated and directing all consumers to the v2 API reference documentation.
A link to the full v2 API specification - consumers can diff the specs themselves to understand all differences.

Step-by-step instructions mapping v1 request/response patterns to v2 equivalents, with code examples in common languages/frameworks, an explicit field mapping table for renamed or removed fields, a summary of authentication changes, and the migration timeline. Ideally also includes a compatibility layer or coexistence period.
questions.explanation: Option D describes the complete migration guide standard. A migration guide is a separate deliverable from the API reference - it is a step-by-step transition document, not a specification replacement. Migration guide section What it must answer Overview of changes What changed and why - gives consumers context for the migration scope Field mapping table Old field name → New field name / Removed (no replacement) / Consolidated into X Code examples Before/after code in the languages most commonly used to call the API Auth changes If authentication or scopes changed, the migration of auth is often the hardest part Timeline Exact dates for each deprecation phase; no ambiguity Support channel Where to ask questions: Slack channel, support email, office hours Why pointing to the reference doc is insufficient: Consumers already know the v2 reference doc exists. What they need is the delta - specifically what they need to change in their existing integration. A good migration guide takes 80% of the work out of migration planning.

questions.q: A public API with 5,000 registered third-party developers is being deprecated. Which notification strategy is most appropriate?
options: Deprecate the endpoint immediately with a 410 Gone status - developers are contractually obligated to monitor changelog RSS feeds.
A silent API change - add Deprecation and Sunset response headers and wait for developers to notice them in their monitoring tools.

Multi-channel approach: email all registered developers directly with the deprecation timeline and migration guide, publish a changelog entry, display a deprecation banner in the developer dashboard, return Deprecation and Sunset HTTP response headers. Provide a 6-12 month migration window. Offer migration support (office hours or dedicated support) for high-usage consumers.
Post a single blog post and update the developer documentation - this is the standard approach for public API deprecation.
questions.explanation: Option C describes the multi-channel approach required for a public API deprecation at scale. No single communication channel reaches all developers: Channel Who it reaches Coverage gap if omitted Direct email to registered devs Developers who provided an email on signup Developers who don't monitor changelog or HTTP headers Changelog / release notes Developers who actively monitor changelogs Most developers don't check changelogs proactively Developer dashboard banner Developers who log in to the portal Developers using only API keys without portal access HTTP deprecation headers Automated monitoring tools in developer systems Teams without automated API monitoring High-usage consumer support: Developers with thousands of daily API calls should receive proactive outreach - an account manager contact or dedicated Slack channel. A large enterprise consumer breaking after sunset can create significant business impact for both parties.

questions.q: An API team is renaming the required request field customer_id to account_id in the POST /orders endpoint. Which announcement phrase most accurately communicates the impact to consumer engineering teams?
options: "Breaking change: the required request field 'customer_id' has been renamed to 'account_id' in POST /orders. Integrations sending 'customer_id' will receive 400 Bad Request after [date]. Action required: update your integration to use 'account_id' before [date]. See the migration guide at [link]."
"The checkout API has been improved. The field naming is now consistent with our new account model."
"The POST /orders endpoint has been updated for consistency with our new data model. Please review the updated API documentation."
"Minor update to POST /orders - a field alias has been added for backward compatibility with legacy field names."
questions.explanation: Option A is the correct announcement format for a breaking change. It contains every element a developer team's engineer needs to act on immediately: Element Example in Option A Why it's required Breaking change label "Breaking change:" Engineers scan changelogs for this keyword - it must be prominent Specific change "'customer_id' renamed to 'account_id' in POST /orders" Engineers need to know exactly what changed to assess their specific integration Failure mode "will receive 400 Bad Request" Engineers need to know what their integration will do if they don't act Effective date "after [date]" Gives a clear deadline for sprint planning and prioritisation Action required "update your integration to use 'account_id'" Removes ambiguity about what the developer must actually do Migration guide link "See migration guide at [link]" Points to detailed instructions without requiring the announcement to be exhaustive

questions.q: Reviewer: 'Okay, I've spotted a potential issue with the upcoming changes to the /users/{user_id}/profile endpoint. The documentation states it will be marked as deprecated in three months, but there's no mention of what happens to existing user profiles at that point. Should we add a clear message to the PR describing the data migration process and any potential downtime impacts?', Which response would best address this reviewer's concern during the code review discussion?
options: 'We're aware of the deprecation timeline. The existing profiles will be read-only after sunsetting; new profile updates won't be accepted.'
'The team is working on a rollback plan in case the migration fails. We'll keep you updated on the progress.'
'Thanks for flagging that! We've scheduled a separate migration task to handle data conversion, and we'll update the documentation shortly.'
Insufficient - simply stating 'endpoint being deprecated' is sufficient for a code review comment.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the importance of proactive communication during API deprecation. Option D is too vague and doesn't address the reviewer's specific concern about data handling. Option C acknowledges the problem but deflects responsibility without offering concrete information. Option A provides a technically accurate but potentially alarming description of the future state, which isn't helpful for guiding development decisions. Option B introduces unnecessary complexity (rollback plans) that isn't central to the immediate communication need - the key is to outline *what* will happen with existing data.

questions.q: Team Lead: 'Okay, the team's been working on the PaymentGateway.v1 API. We're planning to officially deprecate it in six months and switch to the new PaymentGateway.v2 which offers improved security and performance. However, I've noticed several client apps still heavily rely on this endpoint for processing payments. What's the MOST effective way to communicate this change proactively to our developer community?', Which of the following actions should the team prioritize?
options: Okay … scheduling a brief meeting with the core development team to discuss the changes internally before notifying external clients.
… sending a single email announcement to all registered developers.
Good … simply updating the API's status in our internal tracking system and letting developers discover the change through normal API updates.
Excellent … publishing a detailed deprecation notice on the API portal with links to migration guides and updated documentation, alongside proactive outreach to key client accounts.
questions.explanation: The best approach is option 1 because proactive communication involving multiple channels is crucial for successful API deprecation. Simply sending an email won't be sufficient; a comprehensive strategy including a detailed notice on the portal, migration guides, and targeted outreach to key clients demonstrates commitment and provides developers with the necessary resources to adapt. Options 2, 3, and 4 are all inadequate - they lack the breadth of communication needed for a significant API change impacting a diverse developer base. A phased approach is vital to minimize disruption.

questions.q: During a Slack discussion about the upcoming deprecation of the /v1/products endpoint, a developer asks: 'What's the best way to let our users know we're changing things and what they need to do?' Here are some options: A. 'Just remove the endpoint - it's self-explanatory!' B. 'We'll send an email announcing the change, but no need for anything more detailed.' C. 'Let's create a comprehensive API deprecation notice outlining the new endpoint, migration steps, and potential downtime impacts, along with clear documentation updates.' D. 'Don't worry about it; most developers will figure it out eventually.'

exercises.title: API Design Patterns Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Learn API design patterns vocabulary: resource hierarchy, collection vs. singleton resources, sub-resources vs. query parameters, RPC-style endpoints, HATEOAS - for fluent API design discussions.

questions.q: The API designer says: 'We model this as a collection resource under /orders.' What is a 'collection resource' in REST?
options: A resource that aggregates data from multiple microservices
A resource representing a list of items of the same type, typically accessed with GET returning an array
A resource that is read-only and cannot be modified
A resource protected by API key authentication
questions.explanation: A collection resource represents a set of items of the same type. For example, /orders is a collection resource. You can GET the whole collection, POST to add a new item, and access individual items via /orders/{id} (a singleton resource). The distinction matters for naming, HTTP method semantics, and pagination design.

questions.q: A colleague says: 'Use sub-resources for things that only exist in the context of their parent.' Which URL pattern correctly uses a sub-resource?
options: /comments?postId=123
/posts/123/comments
/posts-comments/123
/resources/posts/all/comments
questions.explanation: /posts/123/comments is the correct sub-resource pattern. Comments in this design only exist in the context of post 123. Sub-resources express containment or strong ownership. Query parameters like ?postId=123 are more appropriate for optional filtering of independent resources.

questions.q: The tech lead comments: 'This operation doesn't fit REST - consider an RPC-style endpoint.' When is an RPC-style endpoint appropriate?
options: When the operation is a standard CRUD action on a named resource
When the operation is an action or command that doesn't map cleanly to creating, updating, or deleting a resource
When the API needs to support pagination
When the endpoint must return data in XML format
questions.explanation: RPC-style endpoints (e.g., POST /orders/123/cancel) are appropriate for actions or commands - like cancel, approve, send - that are not straightforward resource mutations. Forcing every action into REST resource semantics can produce awkward or misleading API designs. RPC-style is acceptable when the action doesn't map naturally to a resource lifecycle.

questions.q: The architect mentions HATEOAS in the API design review. What does HATEOAS mean?
options: High Availability Through Enterprise Architecture Systems
Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State
HTTP Advanced Transformation Engine and Object Architecture Schema
Hierarchical API Token Exchange and Authorisation System
questions.explanation: HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State. It is a REST constraint where API responses include links to related actions and resources, allowing clients to navigate the API dynamically without hardcoding URLs. For example, an order response might include links to 'cancel', 'ship', and 'invoice' actions based on the current state.

questions.q: During a design review, the engineer asks: 'Should we use sub-resources or query parameters for filtering orders by status?' What is the recommended approach?
options: Sub-resources: /orders/status/pending
Query parameters: /orders?status=pending
A separate collection resource: /pending-orders
A POST request with a filter body: POST /orders/filter
questions.explanation: Query parameters are the standard approach for filtering a collection resource by attribute values. /orders?status=pending is idiomatic REST. Sub-resources express structural relationships (e.g., /orders/123/items), not attribute filtering. Using sub-resources for filter values (e.g., /orders/status/pending) conflates navigation with filtering.

questions.q: PR Description Subject: Implement new user profile endpoint Body: Hi team, This PR introduces a new endpoint for retrieving and updating user profiles. We're using a nested resource structure to organize the data, with /users/{userId}/profile . Reviewers, please focus on ensuring the response format adheres to the API contract defined in the Swagger spec. Let me know if you have any questions! -John
options: insufficient - the PR lacks documentation for the new endpoint's usage.
correct - the nested resource structure is a standard practice for complex data models and simplifies retrieval of user profile information.
incorrect - using a single endpoint /users/{userId} would be more RESTful, as it avoids nesting and aligns with the principle of resources being independent entities.
incorrect - the PR should include examples of how to use the new endpoint in client-side code for easier integration.
questions.explanation: This scenario presents a common situation during code reviews. The question tests understanding of when and why nested resource structures are used in API design. It's correct because nesting is often appropriate for data that logically belongs to a parent resource (the user) and has associated properties (the profile). Options A, C, and D misinterpret the purpose or RESTful principles involved; simply stating it's 'standard practice' doesn't explain *why* it's suitable here.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm a little concerned about this API design. We've created a resource hierarchy - a top-level `users` collection and then sub-resources for each user's profile. While it seems logical, is there a specific reason we aren't leveraging more explicit relationships within the API itself, perhaps through HATEOAS links? It feels like we're just nesting resources without explicitly stating how to navigate them.' Considering this feedback, which statement best captures the primary benefit of implementing a resource hierarchy, particularly when considering broader API discoverability and maintainability? Consider that simply nesting resources doesn't inherently solve navigation problems. A well-designed API should guide clients towards related data.
options: Insufficient - relying solely on client-side logic for navigating the hierarchy will lead to inconsistencies and errors over time.
Correct - a resource hierarchy provides a clear, intuitive structure that simplifies client development by reducing the need for complex URL manipulation.
Incorrect - HATEOAS is always superior to a simple resource hierarchy and should be used regardless of the complexity of the API.
Irrelevant - the reviewer's concern about discoverability is a minor issue compared to the technical correctness of the implementation.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights that a resource hierarchy provides a clear and intuitive structure for clients. This reduces the complexity of URL manipulation required by the client-side code. The other options represent misconceptions: simply nesting resources doesn't *guarantee* discoverability, HATEOAS is an *additional* technique (and not always superior), and the reviewer's concern, while valid, isn't the core benefit being described here. A good API design should make navigation obvious, and a hierarchy facilitates this by grouping related data logically.

exercises.title: 🔍 API Design Review Language

questions.q: An architect proposes an API-first workflow: "We write the OpenAPI specification before any implementation code is written. Both the backend team and frontend team work against the spec from day one." What is the primary advantage of this approach over an implementation-first approach?
options: Writing the spec upfront guarantees the implementation will be correct and bug-free, because any developer can verify their implementation against the spec document.

The API-first approach is only valuable for public or third-party-facing APIs. For internal APIs consumed exclusively by first-party clients, an implementation-first approach always delivers faster results with less process overhead.

Writing the spec before implementation enables parallel frontend and backend development against a shared contract; catches interface design problems before they are baked into code; creates a shared vocabulary that prevents scope misunderstanding; and allows consumer teams to give feedback on API design choices before any path-dependent development decisions are made.

The OpenAPI specification becomes a legally binding contract between provider and consumer teams, meaning the API cannot deviate from the spec at any point without a formal change management process through all impacted teams.
questions.explanation: Option C correctly identifies the core advantages of API-first (also called "spec-first" or "design-first") development. The other options contain common misconceptions: Claim Why it's wrong A: guarantees bug-free implementation A spec establishes the interface contract , not implementation correctness. Bugs in business logic, data processing, or edge cases are independent of spec quality. B: only useful for public APIs Internal APIs benefit equally - parallel development speed gains apply regardless of who consumes the API. Many teams find internal API contracts more important because there is no external documentation discipline forcing clarity. D: legally binding, no deviations A spec is a living design document, not a legal contract. Agile workflows expect iterative spec updates as understanding improves. The goal is early alignment, not contractual rigidity. API-first benefits summary: Parallel development - frontend can build against a mock server generated from the spec while backend implements Design feedback - stakeholders (mobile, web, data teams) can review the API design before code is written and difficult to change Shared language - "resource", "field name", "endpoint path" are agreed before ambiguous verbal communication causes drift Contract testing - automated validation that implementation matches the spec catches regressions early

questions.q: A developer proposes returning HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) links in all API responses - for example, a GET /orders/{id} response would include a _links object with URLs for cancel , refund , invoice actions. When does HATEOAS add genuine value, and when is it over-engineering?
options: HATEOAS adds genuine value when clients navigate the API dynamically without hardcoded prior knowledge - for example, a generic API browser or a workflow-driven API where the available next actions depend on the current resource state. It is over-engineering for internal APIs with stable, well-known contracts, or when all consumers are first-party clients built with full knowledge of all API endpoints.

HATEOAS is universally required to reach Richardson Maturity Level 3, and because Level 3 is the highest REST maturity, all APIs should implement HATEOAS to achieve the best possible API design score.

HATEOAS is only appropriate for browser-facing APIs where the links will be rendered as actual clickable HTML anchor elements. For JSON API consumers, the hypermedia links are never used and add unnecessary response payload size.

HATEOAS is a deprecated pattern from the early 2010s that has been functionally replaced by GraphQL introspection, which provides the same discovery capability with better tooling support and type safety.
questions.explanation: Option A correctly identifies when HATEOAS solves a real problem versus when it adds complexity without benefit. The other options contain factual errors: Claim Why it's wrong B: universally required for RMM Level 3 Richardson Maturity Model Level 3 describes HATEOAS, but RMM is a descriptive model , not a prescription. Reaching Level 3 is not a goal in itself - it's one way to model an API. Many excellent, widely-used APIs operate at Level 2 by design. C: only for browser HTML rendering HATEOAS in JSON APIs (HAL, JSON:API, Siren) is well-established and has nothing to do with HTML rendering. The value is programmatic navigation, not visual rendering of links. D: replaced by GraphQL introspection GraphQL introspection reveals the schema and available queries, but GraphQL and REST are different paradigms. Neither replaces the other, and HATEOAS remains a valid REST-style pattern for dynamic navigation use cases. When HATEOAS is the right choice: Generic API consumers (SDKs that navigate multiple APIs without hardcoded knowledge) Workflows with server-driven state machines (order lifecycle with state-dependent actions) APIs designed for third-party developers who must not break when endpoints change When HATEOAS is over-engineering: Internal APIs consumed by services you own and deploy together Simple CRUD APIs with stable, predictable endpoints Tight-coupling scenarios where the client and server are always deployed simultaneously

questions.q: A tech lead says: "We should implement RFC 7807 Problem Details for all error responses." What does an RFC 7807-compliant error response contain, and how does it differ from a simple {"error": "Not found"} ?
options: RFC 7807 is an informal SOAP standard that has been informally adopted by REST APIs. Because it originated in the SOAP community, it uses an XML envelope for error details, which must be converted to JSON by a middleware layer before reaching modern JSON API consumers.

RFC 7807 only standardises the format of 404 Not Found responses. For all other status codes, teams are free to use any error format; consistent formatting across all error types is a team convention, not a standards requirement.

RFC 7807 specifies that error responses should always use HTTP status 200 OK with an is_error: true field, because using 4xx/5xx codes causes some proxy servers and CDNs to strip the response body, potentially losing error detail.

RFC 7807 defines a standard structure containing a type (a URI that identifies the error type and links to documentation), title (a short human-readable description of the error type), status (the HTTP status code), detail (a human-readable explanation of this specific occurrence), and an optional instance (a URI for this specific error occurrence). This allows programmatic error type identification, structured logging, and doc linking vs. an opaque string.
questions.explanation: Option D accurately describes RFC 7807 "Problem Details for HTTP APIs" (also updated by RFC 9457). questions.q: A tech lead says: "For the activity feed endpoint, we should use cursor-based pagination rather than offset-based pagination." Why is cursor-based pagination specifically preferred for feed endpoints over offset-based ( ?page=2&limit=20 )?
options: Cursor-based pagination is always faster and more performant than offset pagination for all dataset sizes, because cursor pagination uses binary search internally while offset pagination uses linear search.
Offset-based pagination is not supported in standard HTTP/1.1 query parameters and causes 400 Bad Request errors on strict RFC-compliant servers.

Offset-based pagination requires the client to manually manage the sort order of results on each request, which creates additional client-side complexity that cursor pagination removes by handling sort order on the server.

Offset pagination has two fundamental problems for feeds: (1) page drift - if items are inserted or deleted between requests, page 2 may skip or repeat items that were on page 1; (2) performance - OFFSET N forces the database to scan and discard N rows before returning results, becoming progressively slower at high offsets. Cursor pagination uses a stable position marker (timestamp, ID, or opaque token) that gives consistent results regardless of concurrent writes and avoids the full-scan penalty.
questions.explanation: Option D explains both the correctness problem (page drift) and the performance problem (O(N) scan) that make offset pagination unsuitable for real-time feeds. questions.q: An architect states: "Rate limiting and JWT authentication validation should both live in the API gateway layer, not be implemented separately in each microservice." Which design principle or pattern is this recommendation based on?
options: Cross-cutting concerns - capabilities that apply uniformly across all services with no service-specific business logic - should be handled once at the infrastructure layer (API gateway) rather than duplicated across every service. Duplicating auth and rate limiting in each service creates inconsistency between implementations, increases maintenance burden, multiplies attack surface, and causes version drift. This is also called the gateway offloading pattern and applies the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle at the architectural level.

JWT tokens can only be validated by the issuing authentication server due to the cryptographic key requirements. Routing every request through a central validation endpoint at the gateway creates latency but is the only architecturally correct approach.

The Microservices Independence Principle states that each service must be fully self-contained, including all authentication and authorisation logic. Centralising auth in the gateway creates a single point of failure that can take down the entire platform if the gateway becomes unavailable.

Principle of Least Privilege - each microservice should only have access to the minimum authentication tokens it requires. Centralising auth at the gateway violates this principle because the gateway handles credentials for all services simultaneously.
questions.explanation: Option A correctly identifies the gateway offloading pattern , which applies cross-cutting concern separation and DRY at the architectural level. The other options contain specific technical errors: Claim Why it's wrong B: JWTs can only be validated by the issuing server JWTs are self-contained by design - the signature is validated using the issuer's public key (asymmetric JWTs) or shared secret (symmetric). API gateways routinely validate JWTs without calling the issuing server, which is one of the core JWT use cases. C: Microservices Independence Principle requires service-level auth Microservice independence refers to deployment, scaling, and data independence - not to duplicating infrastructure concerns. No recognised microservices principle requires auth duplication. The fear of a single point of failure is addressed via gateway redundancy, not service-level auth duplication. D: Principle of Least Privilege violated Principle of Least Privilege is about which resources a principal can access, not about where validation occurs. The gateway validating a JWT does not grant the gateway any additional access rights - it only confirms the token's validity before forwarding the request. If no → gateway. If yes → service.

exercises.title: API Error Handling Vocabulary Quiz
exercises.subtitle: Practice API error handling vocabulary: error response shape, RFC 7807 Problem Details, idempotency key, Retry-After header, and surfacing upstream errors.

questions.q: What does RFC 7807 Problem Details define?
options: A protocol for reporting HTTP server crashes
A standardized JSON error response format with fields: 'type', 'title', 'status', 'detail', and 'instance' for machine-readable error responses
A specification for HTTP status code ranges
A standard for API versioning in error responses
questions.explanation: RFC 7807 defines a standard JSON (and XML) format for HTTP API errors. The 'type' is a URI identifying the error class, 'title' is a short description, 'status' is the HTTP status code, 'detail' is a human-readable explanation, and 'instance' is a URI for the specific occurrence.

questions.q: What is an 'idempotency key' and why do APIs use it?
options: A key used to encrypt API requests for security
A client-generated unique ID included in a request so the server can detect and safely ignore duplicate retries, returning the original response
A key that identifies the API version used in the request
A secret key that must match on both client and server to prevent replay attacks
questions.explanation: An idempotency key lets clients safely retry requests - especially important for payment APIs. If the same idempotency key is seen twice, the server returns the original response without processing the operation again, preventing double charges.

questions.q: An API responds with a 'Retry-After' header. What should the client do?
options: Immediately retry the request ignoring the header
Wait the specified number of seconds (or until the specified date/time) before retrying the request
Report the error to the API support team
Switch to a different API endpoint
questions.explanation: The Retry-After header, typically sent with 429 Too Many Requests or 503 Service Unavailable, tells clients how long to wait before retrying. Clients should respect this value to avoid worsening rate limit or overload situations.

questions.q: A colleague says 'we surface the upstream error.' What does this mean in an API context?
options: The API publishes error logs to a public dashboard
The API passes through the error from a downstream dependency to the caller, rather than wrapping or masking it
The API displays errors in the user interface surface
The API logs errors to a cloud surface monitoring tool
questions.explanation: 'Surfacing the upstream error' means the API relays the error received from a downstream service (like a payment processor or database) to the caller - either verbatim or lightly wrapped - rather than returning a generic 500 that hides the root cause.

questions.q: What is the 'error response shape' in API design?
options: The visual styling of error messages in the developer portal
The consistent JSON structure used for all error responses from an API - including fields like error code, message, and details
The HTTP status code range used for errors
The shape of the error in the API schema validation
questions.explanation: The error response shape is the agreed structure of all error payloads from an API. Consistency matters: clients should be able to handle any error from the API using the same parsing logic, regardless of which endpoint generated it.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'The `createUser` endpoint is returning a 409 Conflict with a Problem Details that says 'Resource already exists'. This should be handled more gracefully - perhaps by logging the attempt and returning a 429 Too Many Requests to the client instead of throwing an exception. It's confusing for the front-end team.' Which of the following best describes the reviewer's concern and suggested approach?
options: A: The reviewer is suggesting the front-end should directly handle the 409 error by displaying a user-friendly message about duplicate records. This is the most direct solution.

B: The reviewer believes returning a 429 Too Many Requests indicates the API rate limit has been exceeded, and the client should retry after a delay-a common strategy for transient errors. This aligns with best practices for handling resource conflicts.
C: The reviewer is advocating for changing the `createUser` endpoint to return a 500 Internal Server Error, as this indicates a more severe server-side issue.
D: The reviewer suggests ignoring the 409 error completely and continuing the creation process, as it's likely the user is simply trying to create an account multiple times.
questions.explanation: The reviewer's suggestion of a 429 Too Many Requests response is crucial because a 409 Conflict signifies a *resource contention* issue - the resource already exists. Returning a 429 signals to the client that they should implement retry logic with a delay (e.g., exponential backoff) which is a standard pattern for handling transient errors like this. Simply returning an exception or displaying a generic error message doesn't address the underlying problem and can lead to poor user experience. Options A, C, and D misinterpret the 409 response and don't align with best practices for API error handling.

questions.q: Slack Message: @john.doe 'The API keeps throwing a 409 error when I try to create a new product. The Problem Details say 'Resource already exists'. It's really confusing for the UI team because they don't know how to handle it.' Which of the following best describes John Doe's issue and the most appropriate response from a technical lead?
options: John is simply reporting a bug; the API documentation should be updated to clearly state that resources cannot be duplicated. insufficient

John is experiencing a common scenario - a conflict due to duplicate resource creation - and needs guidance on how to handle the 409 error gracefully, potentially by logging the attempt and informing the front-end team. correct
The 409 error is a standard HTTP status code indicating a conflict; John should simply retry the request until it succeeds. misinterpretation
John's concern highlights a design flaw in the API that requires immediate redesign to prevent duplicate resource creation. over-reaction
questions.explanation: John is encountering a typical scenario where an API returns a 409 Conflict when attempting to create a resource that already exists. The key here isn't just reporting the error but understanding *why* it's happening and how to handle it effectively. Returning a 429 Too Many Requests (as suggested) is a good approach for rate limiting and providing the front-end team with guidance on retry behavior, aligning with best practices for API design and error handling.

questions.q: Code Review Comment Reviewer: 'The updateProfile endpoint is returning a 400 Bad Request with a Problem Details that says 'Invalid input data'. The client isn't providing any specific validation errors, just this generic message. This makes it incredibly difficult for the front-end team to debug and guide the user on what needs to be corrected.'
options: Insufficient - the server simply rejected the request without explanation.

The reviewer believes the API should return a more detailed error response, perhaps including a list of specific validation failures. ErrorResponse object should include fields like 'field' and 'message'.
The reviewer is suggesting that the front-end team should handle all 400 errors themselves by displaying a generic message to the user.
This situation is perfectly acceptable; the API adheres to REST principles by returning a standard 400 error.
questions.explanation: The reviewer's concern centers around the lack of specific validation information within the 400 Bad Request response. A well-designed API should provide granular detail about what went wrong with the input data - this is crucial for front-end debugging and user experience. Returning a generic 'Invalid input data' message without further context hinders effective error handling and makes it difficult to guide the user toward correction. ErrorResponse objects are designed for exactly this purpose.

exercises.title: API Idempotency Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Master API idempotency vocabulary: idempotent HTTP methods, idempotency key header, safe vs. idempotent vs. neither, retry-safe operations - essential for professional API design discussions.

questions.q: The API designer says: 'The PUT request is idempotent but POST is not.' What does 'idempotent' mean in this context?
options: The request is faster than a POST request
Calling the operation multiple times produces the same result as calling it once
The request is authenticated with an API key
The operation cannot be reversed once executed
questions.explanation: An idempotent operation produces the same result no matter how many times it is called. PUT is idempotent because sending the same PUT request repeatedly sets the resource to the same state each time. POST is not idempotent because each call typically creates a new resource.

questions.q: The engineer says: 'We need to add an idempotency key header to the payment endpoint.' What is the purpose of an idempotency key?
options: To encrypt the payment data in transit
To allow the client to retry the same request safely without creating duplicate operations
To identify which API version the client is using
To limit the rate of requests from a single client
questions.explanation: An idempotency key is a unique value (typically a UUID) that the client includes in the request header. If the same key is sent again, the server recognises it as a duplicate and returns the cached result instead of processing the operation again - making retries safe.

questions.q: A colleague explains: 'A safe HTTP method has no side effects.' Which of the following HTTP methods is both safe AND idempotent?
options: POST
PUT
GET
PATCH
questions.explanation: GET is both safe and idempotent. 'Safe' means the method does not modify the server state. 'Idempotent' means repeated calls have the same effect. GET merely retrieves data. PUT is idempotent but not safe (it modifies state). POST is neither safe nor idempotent.

questions.q: The team discusses: 'These retry-safe operations need special handling.' What makes an operation 'retry-safe' in API design?
options: The operation completes in under 100 milliseconds
The operation can be retried on network failure without risking duplicate side effects
The operation requires no authentication token
The operation is cached on the CDN layer
questions.explanation: A retry-safe operation can be repeated - whether due to network timeout, client retry logic, or infrastructure failure - without causing unintended duplicate effects (such as double-charging a customer). Idempotency keys and idempotent HTTP methods are the main tools for achieving retry safety.

questions.q: During a code review, the reviewer comments: 'PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent by default.' In what situation would a PATCH request NOT be idempotent?
options: When the PATCH request includes a JSON body
When the PATCH applies an absolute value replacement to a field
When the PATCH applies a relative operation such as incrementing a counter
When the PATCH request is sent over HTTPS
questions.explanation: PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent. If a PATCH applies a relative operation (for example, 'increment quantity by 1'), repeated calls will produce different results. If a PATCH sets an absolute value ('set quantity to 5'), it behaves idempotently. The key distinction is relative vs. absolute mutations.

questions.q: PR Description Subject: Implement User Profile Update Endpoint Body: Hi Team, I've implemented a new endpoint to update user profiles via a `PUT` request. The documentation states that this endpoint is designed to be idempotent, ensuring multiple identical requests result in the same final state. I've included an idempotency key header as part of the request, just to be extra cautious. Please review. Thanks, John
options: Insufficient - the PUT request could still unintentionally overwrite data if not handled correctly.
Correct - including the idempotency key guarantees that repeated identical requests will only update the profile once, regardless of network issues or client errors.
Incorrect - 'idempotent' solely refers to whether a single request can be safely retried without unintended side effects; it doesn't account for how multiple identical requests are handled.
Incorrect - The idempotency key is redundant since the PUT request itself is inherently idempotent.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of *how* idempotency translates into practical API design. While knowing the definition of 'idempotent' is important, this scenario highlights that it's not just about a single request; it's about consistent behavior across multiple identical requests. The inclusion of an idempotency key in the PR description demonstrates an awareness of this requirement and reinforces the concept - the correct answer explains precisely how this implementation aligns with the stated goal.

questions.q: During a Slack discussion about the new user profile update API, Sarah says: 'I'm concerned that if a client sends multiple identical `PUT` requests to update the same user's email address, we might end up with inconsistent data. The documentation claims this endpoint is idempotent.' What potential problem is Sarah highlighting regarding idempotency in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Sarah is correctly identifying the core issue with idempotency: multiple identical requests *could* lead to unintended consequences. While `PUT` requests are designed to be idempotent, it doesn't automatically prevent problems if the API logic isn't carefully implemented to handle duplicate updates consistently. The key here is that idempotency guarantees a specific outcome, regardless of how many times the request is sent-it doesn't guarantee the *implementation* of the update process will remain consistent.

questions.q: John implemented a new user profile update endpoint using a `PUT` request and claims it's idempotent. During a standup, he explains: 'The PUT request is designed to be idempotent, meaning multiple identical requests should always result in the same final state of the user profile.' David , a junior developer, asks: 'But what if a client sends *three* identical `PUT` requests trying to change the same user's name? Shouldn't we worry about potential data inconsistencies?'
options: Insufficient - idempotency only applies to GET requests.
Correct - idempotency guarantees consistency regardless of the number of identical requests.
Incorrect - idempotency means a single request should always achieve the same result, but multiple identical requests are still possible if the underlying system isn't designed correctly.
Incorrect - idempotency is irrelevant when dealing with mutable data; any repeated update will have the desired effect.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of idempotency's core principle. John 's statement accurately describes the *goal* of idempotency - that a single request should always produce the same outcome. However, it doesn't fully address David 's concern about multiple identical requests. The correct answer acknowledges this; idempotency guarantees consistency for *a single* identical request, but doesn't inherently prevent multiple identical requests from occurring if the system isn't designed to handle them gracefully (e.g., with proper versioning or conflict resolution).

questions.q: During a standup, Mark says: 'We've implemented an idempotency key for the user update endpoint. It's a string that clients include in every request to help us track and prevent duplicate updates.' Emily, another developer, asks: 'But what happens if the idempotency key itself changes between requests? Does that still guarantee idempotency?'
options: insufficient - the idempotency key is not properly validated.
correct - a changing key always indicates a new request requiring processing.
incorrect - a changing key *should* invalidate the idempotency mechanism and trigger a new operation.
correct - the idempotency key acts as a unique identifier, ensuring identical requests are processed only once regardless of key changes.
questions.explanation: The core principle of idempotency is that an operation should have the same effect whether it's executed multiple times. A changing idempotency key fundamentally breaks this guarantee because each key represents a distinct request. While systems *can* use keys to track requests and prevent duplicates, a changing key means the system has no reliable way to determine if a currently received request is a repeat of a previous one - therefore, it's incorrect to assume idempotency in that scenario. Options A and B represent misunderstandings about how idempotency keys are intended to function.

questions.q: During a code review, Liam comments on John's user profile update endpoint: 'While you've included an idempotency key header, just ensuring the request *looks* identical isn't enough. A truly idempotent operation should guarantee the same outcome regardless of the number of times it's executed.' Considering this feedback, what is Liam primarily criticizing about John's implementation?
options: The use of a PUT request is inherently non-idempotent.
John hasn't properly validated the idempotency key against the server state.
Simply including an idempotency key header doesn't guarantee true idempotency; it only provides a mechanism for detection.
John's implementation correctly uses an idempotency key, but needs more robust error handling.
questions.explanation: Liam is correct in pointing out that simply mimicking the request isn't sufficient. True idempotency requires the server to *remember* and guarantee the same outcome each time, regardless of the number of requests. The idempotency key header only provides a mechanism for detecting duplicates; it doesn't inherently enforce the idempotent behavior on the server side. John needs to ensure his logic correctly handles and remembers the state after each request.

exercises.title: API Pagination Vocabulary Quiz
exercises.subtitle: Practice API pagination vocabulary: cursor-based pagination, offset/limit pagination, page tokens, keyset pagination, results-per-page patterns, and Link header conventions.

questions.q: What is cursor-based pagination in an API?
options: Pagination controlled by a mouse cursor position
Pagination that uses an opaque cursor (a pointer to a specific position in the dataset) so clients request 'the next N items after this cursor', avoiding offset drift
Pagination using database cursor objects directly in the API response
Pagination that only works with SQL databases
questions.explanation: Cursor-based pagination uses an opaque value (like a base64-encoded ID or timestamp) as a position marker. Clients pass this cursor in subsequent requests to get the next page, which is more stable than offset pagination when data changes.

questions.q: An API returns { 'next_cursor': 'abc123' }. How should the client use this value?
options: Decode it to find the last record's ID and use it as a filter
Pass it as the 'after' or 'cursor' parameter in the next request to retrieve the following page of results
Use it as an authentication token for the next call
Cache it locally and ignore it - it is just metadata
questions.explanation: The client should include the next_cursor value in the next request's 'after' (or equivalent) parameter. This tells the server where to start the next page. The client should treat the cursor as opaque and not parse it.

questions.q: What is a key disadvantage of offset/limit pagination compared to cursor-based pagination?
options: Offset pagination is slower because it uses more HTTP headers
Offset pagination can skip or duplicate records when the underlying dataset changes between requests, because the offset is a count rather than a stable position
Offset pagination requires more complex client code
Offset pagination does not support page size customization
questions.explanation: With offset/limit pagination, if a record is inserted or deleted between requests, the offset shifts and clients may receive duplicates or miss records. Cursor-based pagination avoids this by anchoring to a stable record position.

questions.q: What does a 'Link header' provide in an API paginated response?
options: A link to the API's documentation
RFC 5988 Link relations (rel='next', rel='prev', rel='first', rel='last') with ready-to-use URLs for navigating between pages
A link to the server's health check endpoint
A URL for reporting API bugs
questions.explanation: The Link header (defined in RFC 5988/8288) provides hypermedia navigation links - rel='next' and rel='prev' - so clients can paginate without constructing URLs themselves. GitHub's API is a well-known example.

questions.q: A colleague says 'this returns at most N results per page.' What does 'at most' signal about the API?
options: The API always returns exactly N results
The API may return fewer than N results - for example, on the last page or if fewer matching records exist - but will never return more than N
The API returns N results only when the client requests that page size
The API returns N results per second, not per page
questions.explanation: 'At most N results per page' is standard API documentation language indicating the page_size or limit is a maximum, not a guarantee. The last page, sparse datasets, or filtered queries may return fewer results.

questions.q: Liam : "Hey team, I'm getting a huge list of user profiles back from the API. It's taking forever to load! Can we just limit the results per page to, say, 100?" Sarah : "I was thinking about using cursor-based pagination instead. It seems more efficient in the long run." Which statement best explains why Sarah's suggestion is potentially better than Liam's proposal?
options: "Limiting results per page (offset/limit) always provides a faster initial response time, regardless of the data size."
"Cursor-based pagination avoids issues with 'key slip,' where clients might inadvertently miss subsequent pages if they don't correctly interpret the cursor value."
"Offset/limit pagination is simpler to implement and understand than cursor-based pagination, making it a more practical choice for this scenario."
"Using a fixed page size (offset/limit) prevents the server from needing to perform complex calculations to determine how many results to return based on the client's request."
questions.explanation: Liam's suggestion of using offset/limit pagination is a common initial approach but can quickly become inefficient with large datasets. 'Key slip' occurs when the client doesn't track the cursor correctly, potentially missing subsequent pages because it assumes the data continues in a linear fashion. Cursor-based pagination avoids this by providing a continuous stream of results based on a unique identifier, ensuring all pages are delivered without requiring the client to manage page numbers or offsets. Therefore, Sarah is correct that cursor-based pagination is more robust and scalable for large datasets.

options: It represents the starting offset for retrieving the next batch of results.
It acts as a unique identifier for each page, enabling efficient retrieval without needing to re-evaluate pagination parameters like limit or offset.
It's used to filter out irrelevant data and ensure only recent user records are returned.
It's a simple way to track the number of pages that have been accessed.
questions.explanation: The `next_cursor` is designed for efficient pagination. It uniquely identifies each page's results, allowing the client to directly request the subsequent page without needing to re-specify the offset or limit. This avoids duplicate processing and significantly improves performance compared to using offset-based approaches.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, Maya reports: 'We're getting errors when trying to retrieve all user profiles - the API is returning too many results at once. We need a more scalable solution.' Which pagination method would be *most* suitable for this situation?
options: Offset/Limit Pagination with a large limit value.
Cursor-based Pagination.
Requesting only the top 10 most active users.
Using a full-text search to find specific user profiles.

Unlike offset/limit where the client must repeatedly adjust the offset as more data is returned, cursors allow the client to seamlessly request all subsequent pages without any changes to the initial request parameters. This avoids the performance bottlenecks associated with scanning through a huge range of offsets.

questions.q: Alex is reviewing a new API endpoint for retrieving customer orders. The API documentation states: 'Use `page` and `pageSize` parameters to control the number of orders returned per request.' Which of the following best describes the *intended* use of these parameters?
options: A) These parameters define a fixed, maximum number of results allowed regardless of the total order count.
B) These parameters allow for flexible control over the size of each page of results, enabling efficient retrieval of large datasets.
C) These parameters are mutually exclusive; only one can be used to specify the desired result set size.
D) These parameters should always be combined with a cursor-based pagination strategy for optimal performance.
questions.explanation: Incorrect options highlight misunderstandings about offset/limit pagination. 'page' and 'pageSize' directly control the *size* of each individual page returned by the API. While cursor-based pagination is often a good practice, these parameters are fundamentally focused on controlling the size of each batch retrieved.

David responds: 'Use cursor-based pagination.' What does David mean by 'cursor-based pagination' in this context?

B) Utilizing an incremental pointer ('cursor') returned with each page of results, allowing clients to request subsequent pages without needing to know the total number of users.
C) Limiting the response size to a fixed amount (e.g., 500 characters) for easier processing by the client application.
D) Employing a complex algorithm to filter and rank user profiles based on relevance.
